title: Clinical Clerkship Experience in Trondheim, Norway
paragraphs: In spring 2025 I did a two-month clinical clerkship at St. Olavs Hospital, attached to the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU). NTNU is in Trondheim, the third largest city in Norway, and in Norway there are also medical schools in the capital Oslo, the second city Bergen, and Tromsø in the north. NTNU is a comprehensive university with a wide range of academic fields, not only medicine but also engineering and the humanities, and being able to interact with students of various faculties and exchange students in the student dormitory enriched my life abroad. At the hospital, charts and examinations were in Norwegian, but many staff and patients spoke English fluently, and thanks to that I could have a fulfilling clerkship. During my stay, the Nordic World Ski Championships were held in Trondheim, and it was also impressive that the whole city was wrapped in a festive mood. In this land where cross-country skiing is rooted as culture, there were many opportunities to warm up to doctors and students through the topic of skiing, and it was a happy experience that skiing, which I had started at university, became a conversation starter.

For the first four weeks I belonged to orthopedic surgery, and each day began around 7:30 in the morning with an X-ray conference. I was overwhelmed by the lively discussion with as many as 40 to 50 doctors taking part. I told the doctor in charge of exchange students what I wanted, rotated through various groups, and was able to come into contact with diverse cases and doctors' viewpoints. In the first week, in the orthopedic emergency outpatient department, I mainly observed and assisted with the initial response to patients with fractures and so on. I was anxious about the clinical clerkship in English, but supported by what I had learned in Japan, UpToDate and the patients' cooperation, I gradually got used to practice. From the second week I belonged to the trauma team and had the opportunity to take part in about 30 operations of various sizes. When I was given the opportunity to do dermal suturing, I felt frustrated at my own inexperience, borrowed suturing instruments and practiced every night. In the operating room, there was a unique custom that during long operations they would prepare juice and a nurse would let me drink it through a straw. A different operation was performed every day, and although studying was hard, every day was stimulating and fun. There were also scenes in which I realized the importance of working with other departments, such as cooperation with a geriatrician managing postoperative delirium in proximal femur fractures. In the last week, observing a different outpatient clinic every day (pediatric orthopedics, spine, knee, diabetic foot lesions and so on), every doctor taught me enthusiastically in English between consultations, to the point that I felt reluctant to leave and wanted to keep learning there.

For the second four weeks I belonged to upper gastrointestinal surgery. The day begins at 7:45 in the morning with an imaging conference, and after finishing rounds in the ICU and on the ward, we split into surgery and outpatient clinic. In the Whipple operations I observed several times, there were scenes in which I was entrusted with the role of assistant, and I tasted tension and happiness at the same time. I also observed PEG and so on, but a method different from what I had seen in Japan was used, and I gained learning through comparison. The outpatient clinic centered mainly on examination of inguinal hernias, but that was interesting too. I was also present when a gastroenterologist taught endoscopy to a young surgeon, which was an unexpected joy for me, who was also interested in a gastroenterology clerkship. What especially remains in my memory from the clerkship period is the Friday morning "surgeons' meeting." Before the imaging conference, surgeons from all over the hospital gather in the cafeteria and chat over breakfast. The purpose is to create connections among surgeons, but I felt it might perhaps be more efficient than drinking parties until late at night. At that time a female doctor whom I usually had no chance to talk to gave me a Norwegian waffle and coffee, which became an unforgettable warm memory. As the clerkship progressed, I began going to outpatient clinics in my free time and asking the reception staff, "Is there an interesting clinic?", and I also went in and out of the emergency outpatient department between operations and after the evening with a resident who guided me sincerely. Because the younger generation in Norway is fluent in English, I was surprised that I could take the history of a 10-year-old patient with abdominal pain in English. I could come into contact with cases peculiar to emergency care, such as testicular torsion and appendectomy, and it was a fulfilling time. In the last week, feeling sad about leaving Norway, I asked the resident every detail of how he balances family, work and research. Meeting this resident was memorable for me, and I was greatly stimulated by his attitude of sincerely enjoying daily learning and learning by observing carefully down to the details, and it became an opportunity to look again at what kind of doctor I want to be.

In Norwegian medical settings it is not rare for doctors to leave work after 15:00, and I got the impression that efficiency of work, such as robots moving around the hospital and voice input for charts, is strongly emphasized. In outpatient clinics many online consultations were also held. Doctors and nurses are in a flat relationship, in the operating room greetings and self-introductions are exchanged every time, and many nurses kindly taught me the procedure of that operation and where to stand in the operating room. Since about 70% of medical students are women, I felt that the idea of gender equality is rooted in the workplace. In addition, many doctors from other countries who had come seeking a better working environment were working there, and the diversity in the medical setting was also impressive. Furthermore, students obtain a limited license from the winter of their fifth year and examine patients, so I felt that clinical clerkships in Norway are more practical.

Through this study abroad I gained a viewpoint from which to see Japanese and Norwegian medicine relatively. For example, I reaffirmed the high level of technology in Japan in the gastrointestinal field, and my motivation to study it further grew. On the other hand, by coming into contact with Norwegian medical settings, I feel I acquired a viewpoint for thinking flexibly about ways of working and how teams should be. Also, during the clerkship I introduced myself at suitable moments and asked to be taught in English, decided which surgeries and clinics to take part in and asked to join them, and the importance of this attitude of creating places of learning by myself suddenly made sense one day, as the meaning of the words my kendo teacher, who usually trains me, used to say: "Acquire the character to compete from the front." One of the major results of this study abroad is that, through the reality that if one acquires Norwegian one can also work there, and the many situations in which English functions as a common language, I became able to think about medicine and ways of working with a broader perspective.

What led me to try this dispatched study abroad was the medical English lectures that I kept attending happily thanks to the cheerful personality of Dr. イッツェル. The lectures I received from the doctors of the Frontier Society, the alumni network of those who studied abroad, were a great learning before departure, and what I had learned in clerkships from the doctors who looked after me at the university and in the clerkship just before study abroad greatly helped my learning in this study abroad. I sincerely thank all the doctors, family and friends who supported this study abroad. I will continue to build up my studies and aim to be a doctor needed by society. I sincerely thank everyone who gave me this opportunity.
